- When sentiment is high (≥0.6) and forecast is rising sharply, reduce overshoot by 5–10% to avoid overreacting to bullish sentiment.
- When sentiment is low (≤0.4) and forecast is falling, avoid excessive downward bias — add 2–5% to prevent premature sell-off.
- If recent price history shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days of decline), model should not overcorrect upward — cap forecast rise at 3–4% above recent peak.
- After a spike (e.g., +5%+ in 3–5 days), forecast should not immediately revert to prior levels — allow 1–2 days of lagged momentum before adjusting.
- If sentiment and price history are trending upward but forecast is flat or declining, increase forecast by 3–5% to reflect sentiment momentum.
- For long-term (30d) forecasts, if sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.7) and price is trending up, allow for 1–2% higher forecast than historical mean — but cap at 10% above recent 10-day high to avoid volatility overcorrection.
